docs.title: Rediska
docs.text:
Rediska is a Redis-compatible in-memory key-value server written in Go, built to learn how Redis works on the inside. It speaks RESP, Redis's wire protocol, so redis-cli, redis-benchmark and Redis client libraries can talk to it.

$ rediska --port 7379
$ redis-cli -p 7379 set name vinay
OK
$ redis-cli -p 7379 get name
"vinay"

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Strings and counters: SET (with EX/PX), GET, APPEND, INCR, DEL, EXPIRE, TTL, stored in Redis's compact encodings (int, embstr, raw).
  • HyperLogLog: PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE, with Redis's sparse and dense representations.
  • Transactions: MULTI, EXEC, DISCARD.
  • Persistence: an append-only file (AOF), replayed at startup.
  • Expiry: lazy expiry on access, plus an active expiry loop.
  • Memory limits: --maxmemory with noeviction, approximate LRU or LFU eviction.
  • Cluster mode: 16384 hash slots, MOVED and CROSSSLOT redirects, and the CLUSTER commands real cluster tools use. See Cluster mode.
  • Redis's threading model: one goroutine per connection, but every command runs on a single dispatch worker, so data needs no locks. See Design decisions.

docs.title: Milestone 15
docs.text:
Cluster bus: nodes check on each other (Phase 4a)

  1. Every node listens on a second port, its client port + 10000, for other nodes only. Messages are RESP arrays, so nc can talk to it
  2. Each node connects to every other node in the layout, retries every second while one is down, and reconnects by itself when it comes back
  3. Nodes send each other PING once a second and answer with PONG
  4. CLUSTER NODES shows real ping-sent and pong-received times, and connected / disconnected
  5. The bus's goroutines only wait and pass events on (EvTick, EvLinkUp, EvMessage, ...). The dispatch worker handles them, so cluster state needs no locks, like the data
  6. The worker never waits on the network: messages go through a per-connection outbox and writer goroutine, and dials through dialLoop
  7. cluster/bus_test.go runs three buses in one process under -race

Try it:

./scripts/cluster.sh start
redis-cli -p 7001 cluster nodes        # pong times move every second
lsof -ti :7002 | xargs kill            # node2 shows disconnected
./scripts/cluster.sh stop

TODO

  1. No gossip or CLUSTER MEET yet: every node reads the full layout (Phase 4b)
  2. No failure detection: a stopped node shows disconnected, but nodes don't agree that it has failed (Phase 4d)
  3. Finding itself by port still only works on one machine

docs.title: Milestone 14
docs.text:
Fixed-layout cluster with redirects (Phase 2)

  1. Each node reads the whole layout from --cluster-config-file (name, address, slot ranges) and finds itself by its port. A broken layout stops the node at startup
  2. Before running a command, the node checks its keys: -> keys in different slots: CROSSSLOT -> slot owned by nobody: CLUSTERDOWN Hash slot not served -> slot owned by another node: MOVED <slot> <host:port>
  3. AOF replay skips the cluster check, so a node always loads its own data
  4. MULTI/EXEC: each command is checked when queued (MOVED -> EXECABORT), and all queued keys must be in one slot at EXEC (CROSSSLOT), so a transaction never runs halfway
  5. Added CLUSTER SLOTS, CLUSTER NODES, CLUSTER MYID, CLUSTER INFO and the # Cluster section in INFO, matching real Redis 7's formats
  6. scripts/cluster.sh start|stop|status|clean runs a local cluster
  7. End-to-end test (go test ./e2e/) starts 3 real nodes and checks redirects, hash tags, pipelines, transactions and CLUSTER SLOTS
  8. Verified with redis-cli -c, redis-cli --cluster check and redis-benchmark --cluster

Try it:

./scripts/cluster.sh start
redis-cli -p 7001 set name vinay      # MOVED 5798 127.0.0.1:7002
redis-cli -c -p 7001 set name vinay   # follows the redirect: OK
redis-cli -p 7001 del age name        # CROSSSLOT
./scripts/cluster.sh stop

TODO

  1. Nodes don't talk to each other yet; the layout is fixed until restart (Phase 4)
  2. No moving slots between nodes (Phase 5), no replicas or failover (Phases 6, 7)
  3. Finding itself by port only works when all nodes are on one machine; needs a --cluster-node-name flag for separate machines
  4. redis-py's cluster client also needs HELLO and COMMAND, which Rediska doesn't have yet

docs.title: Cluster mode
docs.text:
In cluster mode, several Rediska nodes split the keys between them, the way Redis Cluster does. Each node holds only its share, and clients are sent to the right node.

Current scope

The cluster layout is fixed: every node reads it from a file at startup. Nodes check on each other over the cluster bus, but they don't share the layout or detect failures yet, slots can't move while running, and there are no replicas. See Limitations.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text:
Every key belongs to one of 16384 hash slots:

slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384

Each node owns some of the slots, and stores only the keys in them.

flowchart LR
    K1["name"] --> S1["slot 5798"] --> N2["node2 (5461–10922)"]
    K2["age"] --> S2["slot 741"] --> N1["node1 (0–5460)"]
    K3["visits"] --> S3["slot 12263"] --> N3["node3 (10923–16383)"]

There are far more keys than slots, so each slot holds many keys. Slots are the unit that gets assigned to nodes (and, in a later phase, moved between them), so the cluster map stays small: 16384 entries, however many keys you have.

$ redis-cli -p 7001 cluster keyslot name
(integer) 5798

docs.title: Hash tags
docs.text:
If a key contains {...}, only the part inside the braces is hashed. Keys with the same tag always land in the same slot:

$ redis-cli -p 7001 cluster keyslot {user1}.name
(integer) 8106
$ redis-cli -p 7001 cluster keyslot {user1}.email
(integer) 8106

Use hash tags for keys you need to use together in one command or transaction.

docs.title: The layout file
docs.text:
Every node reads the same layout file, which lists every node, its address and the slots it owns:

cluster.conf
# name   address          slots
node1  127.0.0.1:7001  0-5460
node2  127.0.0.1:7002  5461-10922
node3  127.0.0.1:7003  10923-16383
  • Slots can be ranges (0-5460) or single slots (42), several per line.
  • Anything after # is a comment.
  • A node finds its own line by matching its --port.
  • Any mistake (overlapping slots, a slot above 16383, a duplicate name or address, no line for this node's port) stops the node at startup, naming the line.
  • Slots that no line lists are unowned: commands on them get CLUSTERDOWN, while every other slot keeps working.

Start each node with the same file and its own port:

rediska --port 7001 --cluster-enabled --cluster-config-file cluster.conf
rediska --port 7002 --cluster-enabled --cluster-config-file cluster.conf
rediska --port 7003 --cluster-enabled --cluster-config-file cluster.conf

Each node also listens on its client port + 10000 (here 17001–17003) for the cluster bus, so those ports must be free too.

docs.title: The cluster script
docs.text:
scripts/cluster.sh does all of that for you:

./scripts/cluster.sh start     # build, write the layout, start the nodes
./scripts/cluster.sh status    # which nodes are running, and their key counts
./scripts/cluster.sh stop      # stop them; data stays in each node's AOF
./scripts/cluster.sh clean     # stop and delete all their files

Files go in /tmp/rediska-cluster/. NODES=4 ./scripts/cluster.sh start starts 4 nodes with the slots split evenly (run clean first if you change the number of nodes).

docs.title: How a command is routed
docs.text:
Before running a command, a node checks its keys, in the same order as Redis:

flowchart TD
    A[command arrives] --> B{any keys?}
    B -- "no (PING, INFO, ...)" --> RUN[run it here]
    B -- yes --> C{all keys in one slot?}
    C -- no --> X1["CROSSSLOT Keys in request<br/>don't hash to the same slot"]
    C -- yes --> D{does anyone own the slot?}
    D -- no --> X2["CLUSTERDOWN Hash slot not served"]
    D -- yes --> E{is it me?}
    E -- no --> X3["MOVED <slot> <host:port>"]
    E -- yes --> RUN

The error texts match Redis 7 word for word, so clients that understand Redis Cluster understand Rediska:

$ redis-cli -p 7001 set name vinay
(error) MOVED 5798 127.0.0.1:7002
$ redis-cli -c -p 7001 set name vinay
-> Redirected to slot [5798] located at 127.0.0.1:7002
OK
$ redis-cli -p 7001 del age name
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

redis-cli -c follows MOVED redirects for you. In a pipeline, each command gets its own reply, in order.

docs.title: The cluster bus
docs.text:
Every node opens a second port for other nodes, at its client port + 10000 (7001 → 17001). Clients never use it.

Over the bus, each node:

  • connects to every other node in cluster.conf, retrying every second if one isn't up yet
  • sends each connected node a PING once a second, and answers every PING with a PONG
  • notices when a connection closes, shows that node as disconnected, and reconnects by itself when it comes back

Messages use RESP, the same format as client commands. Each one is an array of 7 items: type, the sender's ID, name, address and flags, the sender's own slots (as start/end pairs), and a gossip section listing other nodes. You can talk to the bus by hand:

$ (printf '*7
$4
PING
$1
x
$4
test
$14
127.0.0.1:9999
:0
*0
*0
'; sleep 1) | nc localhost 17001

The reply is a PONG carrying node1's ID, name, address and slots (0 5460). Nodes don't act on the slots or gossip sections yet; they're there for gossip, which comes next.

Bus work runs on the same goroutine as client commands, so cluster state, like the data, needs no locks. See Goroutines in a cluster node for which goroutine does what.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
All keys in a MULTI/EXEC transaction must be in one slot, owned by the node you're connected to. Rediska checks this in two places, as Redis does:

While queuing, each command is checked on its own. If one fails, the transaction is marked broken and EXEC refuses to run anything:

127.0.0.1:7001> multi
OK
127.0.0.1:7001(TX)> set age 30
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:7001(TX)> set name vinay
(error) MOVED 5798 127.0.0.1:7002
127.0.0.1:7001(TX)> exec
(error) EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of previous errors.

At EXEC, all the queued keys are checked together. This catches commands that are fine on their own but use different slots:

127.0.0.1:7001> multi
OK
127.0.0.1:7001(TX)> set age 30
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:7001(TX)> set foo2 x
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:7001(TX)> exec
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

age (slot 741) and foo2 (slot 1044) are both on node1, but in different slots, so the transaction is refused. Either way, a transaction never runs halfway. Use hash tags to keep a transaction's keys together:

127.0.0.1:7002> multi
OK
127.0.0.1:7002(TX)> set {user1}.name vinay
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:7002(TX)> incr {user1}.visits
QUEUED
127.0.0.1:7002(TX)> exec
1) OK
2) (integer) 1

docs.title: CLUSTER commands
docs.text:
Command Returns Used by CLUSTER KEYSLOT key the key's slot debugging CLUSTER COUNTKEYSINSLOT slot how many of this node's keys are in the slot checking how data is spread; moving slots CLUSTER GETKEYSINSLOT slot count up to count of this node's keys in the slot moving slots CLUSTER SLOTS slot ranges and their owners client libraries, to learn the map CLUSTER NODES one line per node redis-cli --cluster, redis-benchmark --cluster CLUSTER MYID this node's 40-character ID debugging CLUSTER INFO cluster_state:ok if every slot has an owner, plus counts monitoring

INFO cluster reports cluster_enabled:1 on a cluster node.

COUNTKEYSINSLOT and GETKEYSINSLOT answer about the node you ask, whoever owns the slot, and never redirect:

$ redis-cli -p 7002 cluster countkeysinslot 8106
(integer) 3
$ redis-cli -p 7002 cluster getkeysinslot 8106 10
1) "{user1}.name"
2) "{user1}.email"
3) "{user1}.visits"
$ redis-cli -p 7001 cluster countkeysinslot 8106
(integer) 0

To answer these quickly, each cluster node keeps a small index of which of its keys are in each slot, next to its data. It's updated whenever a key is created or removed (including by expiry and eviction), and it's switched off on a normal single node.

Node IDs are derived from the node's name, so they stay the same across restarts.

In CLUSTER NODES, the ping-sent and pong-received columns come from the cluster bus. They are Unix times in milliseconds (0 means none pending, or never), and the link state is connected or disconnected. Run it twice: on a healthy cluster, the pong times move forward every second.

docs.title: Tools that work
docs.text:
• redis-cli -c: follows redirects.
  • redis-cli --cluster check 127.0.0.1:7001: reports all 16384 slots covered.
  • redis-benchmark --cluster -p 7001: spreads load across the nodes.

Some client libraries also need commands Rediska doesn't have yet. For example, redis-py's cluster client reads the slot map, then calls COMMAND.

docs.title: Persistence in a cluster
docs.text: Each node has its own AOF, holding only its own keys. When a node restarts, it loads its whole AOF back without the cluster check, so its data is never dropped, even if the layout file changed while it was down.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Fixed layout, no gossip yet: every node learns the layout from cluster.conf and connects to every node in it. There's no CLUSTER MEET; to change the layout, edit the file and restart the nodes.
  • No failure detection yet: a stopped node shows as disconnected, but nodes don't yet agree that it has failed, and routing doesn't change.
  • No slot migration: slots can't move between running nodes.
  • No replicas or failover: if a node goes down, its slots are unavailable until it comes back.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text: Why Rediska is built the way it is. Each section says what was chosen, why, and what it costs.

docs.title: How a command flows
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C1[client] --> G1[connection goroutine]
    C2[client] --> G2[connection goroutine]
    G1 -- "command / pipeline / MULTI batch" --> CH[(channel)]
    G2 --> CH
    E[active expiry, every 100 ms] --> CH
    B[cluster bus] -- "bus events" --> CH
    CH --> W[dispatch worker]
    W --> D[Dispatch:<br/>cluster check, memory check,<br/>handler, AOF]
    D --> S[(store)]
  1. Each client connection has its own goroutine. It reads and parses RESP, handles MULTI queuing, and groups pipelined commands.
  2. Every command that touches data is sent over one channel to a single dispatch worker.
  3. The worker runs commands one at a time: cluster check, memory check, the command's handler, then the AOF write. The reply goes back to the connection.
  4. In cluster mode, the cluster bus sends its events over the same channel, so the worker also runs the bus's decisions, between commands (see Goroutines in a cluster node).

docs.title: One worker goroutine for all data
docs.text:
Choice: every command runs on one goroutine, like Redis's single thread, instead of locking the store.

Why: no locks in the store at all, and commands are atomic for free: nothing can interleave with a command, or with an EXEC batch. It also mirrors how Redis really works, which is the point of the project.

Cost: one CPU core does all the data work. The channel was the main bottleneck under pipelined load, which is why pipelined commands are now sent to the worker as one batch (see Performance).

docs.title: Compact value encodings
docs.text:
Choice: like Redis, a value is stored as a number (int) if it parses as one, and as a string (embstr up to 44 bytes, raw above) otherwise. Each stored value is a small tagged struct, not a Go any.

Why: saves memory, and avoids an allocation per SET that boxing into an interface would cost. OBJECT ENCODING shows which one a key uses.

docs.title: Approximate LRU and LFU by sampling
docs.text:
Choice: eviction samples a few keys (--maxmemory-samples, default 5) and evicts the best candidate from a small pool, like Redis.

Why: exact LRU needs a linked list across every key, which costs memory and time on every access. Sampling gets close to exact behaviour at a tiny cost, which is why Redis does it.

docs.title: Copy Redis Cluster's design
docs.text:
Choice: 16384 slots, CRC16 hashing, {hash tags}, MOVED and CROSSSLOT, and the CLUSTER commands, all matching Redis 7's formats word for word.

Why: existing tools (redis-cli -c, redis-benchmark --cluster, redis-cli --cluster check) work against Rediska unchanged, and each piece maps to a part of Redis you can read about.

docs.title: One shared layout file, read at startup
docs.text:
Choice: every node reads the same cluster.conf.

Why: you can see the whole cluster in one place, and every node is guaranteed to agree. Real Redis has nodes discover each other (gossip), which comes later; doing it in this order keeps redirect bugs and gossip bugs apart.

Cost: changing the layout means editing the file and restarting.

docs.title: Find yourself by port
docs.text:
Choice: a node finds its own line in the layout by its --port.

Why: simplest for running several nodes on one machine.

Cost: doesn't work across machines, where nodes typically all use the same port. A --cluster-node-name flag is the planned fix.

docs.title: Unowned slots fail one at a time
docs.text:
Choice: a slot missing from the layout gets CLUSTERDOWN Hash slot not served; every other slot keeps working. CLUSTER INFO still reports cluster_state:fail, as Redis would.

Why: a mistake in the layout shouldn't take down every key. (Redis's default is to stop serving everything until all slots are covered.)

docs.title: Check before running, never after
docs.text:
Choice: the cluster check happens before a command's handler runs. Out-of-memory checks also run before the handler.

Why: a refused command must have no effect: nothing stored, nothing written to the AOF.

docs.title: Transactions are checked twice
docs.text:
Choice: each command is checked when it's queued, and all queued keys are checked together at EXEC.

Why: that's what Redis does. Checking at queue time tells the client straight away (and MOVED says where to go). Checking at EXEC catches commands that are each fine but use different slots. Together they guarantee a transaction never runs halfway.

Why "same slot", not "same node": slots are what move between nodes. A transaction that only needed "same node" could break later just because a slot moved.

docs.title: AOF replay skips the cluster check
docs.text:
Choice: at startup, commands read back from the AOF run directly, not through the cluster check.

Why: everything in a node's AOF was already accepted by that node. If the layout changed while the node was down, replaying through the check would silently drop those keys.

docs.title: Node IDs from names
docs.text:
Choice: a node's 40-character ID is the SHA-1 of its name.

Why: tools expect IDs of that shape, and deriving them from names keeps them the same across restarts without storing anything.

docs.title: Goroutines in a cluster node
docs.text:
A cluster node runs the goroutines below. Only the dispatch worker reads or changes data and cluster state; every other goroutine waits on something (a socket, a timer, a channel) and passes what happened on.

flowchart LR
    subgraph clients["Client side"]
        CG["connection goroutine<br/>(one per client)"]
        AE["active expiry"]
    end
    subgraph bus["Cluster bus"]
        CR["cronLoop"]
        AL["acceptLoop"]
        DL["dialLoop"]
        DI["dial<br/>(one per attempt)"]
        RL["readLoop<br/>(one per connection)"]
        WR["writer<br/>(one per connection)"]
    end
    CH[("commandCh")]
    W["dispatch worker"]

    CG -- commands --> CH
    AE -- "expiry job" --> CH
    CR -- "EvTick" --> CH
    DI -- "EvLinkUp / EvDialFailed" --> CH
    RL -- "EvMessage / EvLinkDown" --> CH
    CH --> W

    W -- "dialReq (from tick)" --> DL
    DL -- starts --> DI
    DI -- "starts both" --> RL
    DI -. "starts" .-> WR
    AL -- "starts both" --> RL
    W -- "link.send: the outbox" --> WR

Read it left to right: everything flows into commandCh, the worker decides, and it acts on the network only by asking dialLoop for a connection or putting a message in a connection's outbox.

Goroutine Started by How many Waits for Then connection goroutine server.Run one per client the client's next command sends it to the worker active expiry server.Run 1 a 100 ms timer sends an expiry job dispatch worker server.Run 1 the next request on commandCh runs it: a command, or Bus.Handle for a bus event cronLoop Bus.Start 1 a 100 ms timer sends EvTick acceptLoop Bus.Start 1 another node connecting to the bus port starts a readLoop and a writer for it dialLoop Bus.Start 1 a node on dialReq (from tick) starts a dial shutdown helper Bus.Start 1 shutdown closes the bus listener, which stops acceptLoop dial dialLoop one per attempt, short-lived the TCP connection starts a readLoop and a writer, sends EvLinkUp, or EvDialFailed readLoop dial or acceptLoop one per bus connection the next message sends EvMessage; when the connection closes, EvLinkDown writer startLink one per bus connection a message in the outbox writes it to the socket

In a 3-node cluster, each node has 4 bus connections (2 it dialled, 2 dialled to it), so 8 per-connection goroutines plus 4 fixed ones.

docs.title: Bus events go through the dispatch worker
docs.text:
Choice: the bus's goroutines never change cluster state. They describe what happened as an Event (EvTick, EvLinkUp, EvMessage, …) and send it over commandCh, the same channel as client commands. The worker calls Bus.Handle, a single switch that lists every kind of event.

Why: the "one goroutine owns the state" rule now covers cluster state too, so there are no locks there either. Events rather than closures keep every job the bus can ask for in one place, and an event can be logged. The cluster package can't import server (that would be an import cycle), so Bus.Start is handed a func(Event) that knows about commandCh.

Cost: bus work waits its turn behind client commands, so a PING can be a little late under heavy load. Every new kind of bus job needs an event kind and a case in Handle.

docs.title: The worker never waits on the network
docs.text:
Choice: the worker never writes to a socket or dials. To send, it puts the message in the connection's outbox, and that connection's writer goroutine writes it. To connect, tick asks dialLoop, which starts a dial. If an outbox is full, the message is dropped.

Why: a slow or dead node must never stall client commands, which all queue behind the worker. Only dialLoop starts dial goroutines because the worker isn't counted in the bus's WaitGroup: starting goroutines from it could race with Wait at shutdown.

Cost: a message to a stuck node can be lost. That's fine for PING, which is sent again a second later; anything sent over the bus must be safe to lose.

docs.title: Tests start real processes
docs.text:
Choice: the end-to-end test starts three real rediska processes instead of three servers inside one test.

Why: the store and the cluster layout are package-level variables, so three nodes in one process would share one store. Separate processes test exactly what you run. See Testing.

The cluster bus is the exception: a Bus keeps its own state, so cluster/bus_test.go runs three buses in one process, each with a small stand-in for the dispatch worker, under the race detector.

docs.text:
Every release has a .tar.gz (.zip on Windows) for Intel and ARM machines, plus a checksums.txt. Unpack it and put rediska somewhere on your PATH:

tar -xzf rediska_0.1.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz

docs.title: With Go
docs.text:
You need Go 1.25 or newer.

go install github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska@latest

This builds the rediska binary into $(go env GOPATH)/bin, usually ~/go/bin. If your shell can't find rediska afterwards, add that folder to your PATH, for example in ~/.zshrc:

export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

Note

@latest installs the newest tagged release. To try the newest code on the main branch instead, use @main.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
$ rediska --version
rediska 0.1.0 (commit 1a2b3c4, built 2026-10-26T03:00:00Z)

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska
cd rediska
go build -o rediska .
./rediska

You'll also want redis-cli to talk to it. On macOS: brew install redis.

docs.title: Run a single server
docs.text:
rediska --port 7379

In another terminal:

$ redis-cli -p 7379 ping
PONG
$ redis-cli -p 7379 set name vinay EX 60
OK
$ redis-cli -p 7379 ttl name
(integer) 60
$ redis-cli -p 7379 incr visits
(integer) 1
$ redis-cli -p 7379 object encoding visits
"int"

Stop the server with Ctrl+C. It shuts down cleanly: it finishes the commands already in flight and flushes the AOF to disk first.

docs.title: Keep data across restarts
docs.text:
By default, data lives only in memory. To keep it, turn on the append-only file (AOF):

rediska --port 7379 --appendOnly --appendOnlyFile data.aof

Every successful write command is appended to data.aof, and the file is replayed when the server starts.

docs.title: Limit memory
docs.text:
rediska --port 7379 --maxmemory 100 --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

--maxmemory is in megabytes. When the limit is reached:

Policy What happens noeviction (default) writes are refused with an OOM error; reads and DEL still work allkeys-lru the least recently used keys are evicted (approximate, by sampling) allkeys-lfu the least frequently used keys are evicted volatile-lfu currently the same as allkeys-lfu (Redis would only evict keys that have an expiry)

docs.text:
The repository includes a script that starts a 3-node cluster on your machine:

./scripts/cluster.sh start
redis-cli -c -p 7001 set name vinay   # -c follows MOVED redirects
./scripts/cluster.sh stop

See Cluster mode for how it works.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Profiling and closing the gap with Redis.

Benchmarked with redis-benchmark against real Redis on the same machine. Started at roughly half of Redis's throughput and 2x its latency; profiled with pprof at each step rather than guessing, and closed the gap to near parity under pipelined load.

docs.title: 1. Removed unconditional per-command debug logging
docs.text: Two log.Printf calls ran on the hot path for every single command (tcp_server.go), accounting for ~19% of CPU time under load. Removed.

docs.title: 2. Replaced per-command read-deadline polling with a ctx-watcher goroutine
docs.text: The connection loop was calling conn.SetReadDeadline twice per command (~5% of CPU) just to support graceful shutdown. Replaced with a single per-connection goroutine that closes the connection directly when the server's context is cancelled -- removes the syscalls entirely and makes shutdown faster, not slower.

docs.title: 3. Pooled reply channels instead of allocating one per command
docs.text: Each command allocated a fresh chan []byte to receive its reply from the dispatch worker. Replaced with a sync.Pool (~4.7% of CPU).

docs.title: 4. Reduced RESP bulk-string parsing overhead
docs.text:
Combined the body read and trailing \r\n check into a single io.ReadFull call (previously: one ReadFull + two separate ReadByte calls), and added a per-connection reusable scratch buffer so decoding many commands on one connection doesn't allocate a fresh []byte for every argument.

Result of #1-4: roughly 2x throughput, gap to Redis closed from ~2x to ~1.18x (single-command, non-pipelined benchmarking).

docs.title: 5. Batched pipelined commands into a single dispatch round-trip
docs.text:
Profiling with redis-benchmark -P 16 (pipelining) revealed a different bottleneck: every command -- pipelined or not -- was sent through the single dispatch worker as its own message on a Go channel, each paying a full goroutine park/wake + lock cycle. At pipelined request rates this channel contention became the dominant cost, confirmed via CPU profile (pthread_cond_wait/signal and channel-lock functions dominating the profile).

Fixed by accumulating consecutive plain commands already sitting in the connection's read buffer (bufio.Reader.Buffered() > 0, i.e. commands the client already sent without waiting for a reply) into one batch, dispatched through the channel as a single request. MULTI/EXEC transactions and malformed frames are handled correctly as batch boundaries -- verified with targeted tests, not just benchmarked.

Result: pipelined throughput went from ~60k rps to 300k+ rps in local testing, closing the previously channel-contention-dominated gap.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: Profiled with Go's built-in net/http/pprof (enabled via a --pprof-addr flag, off by default) and go tool pprof -http=... for interactive CPU/ allocation flame graphs and call graphs.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
A release is one git tag. Pushing a tag like v0.1.0 makes GitHub Actions:

  1. run the tests (go test -race ./...),
  2. build rediska for macOS, Linux and Windows, each for Intel and ARM,
  3. publish a GitHub Release with the archives, checksums.txt and a changelog of the commits since the last tag,
  4. update the Homebrew cask in vinayhpandya/homebrew-tap, so brew install vinayhpandya/tap/rediska gets the new version.

The workflow is .github/workflows/release.yml, and what gets built is in .goreleaser.yaml. GoReleaser does steps 2–4.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Create the tap repository: a new public repo named exactly homebrew-tap under your account, with a README so it isn't empty. Homebrew finds vinayhpandya/tap by that name.
  2. Create a token for it: on GitHub, Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token. Give it access to only homebrew-tap, with Contents: Read and write.
  3. Store the token in this repo: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret, named HOMEBREW_TAP_GITHUB_TOKEN.

The workflow's built-in GITHUB_TOKEN can only write to this repo, which is why the tap needs its own token. Fine-grained tokens expire, so renew it when GitHub emails you.

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text:
git checkout main && git pull
go test -race ./...            # the workflow does this too, but fail fast
git tag v0.1.0
git push origin v0.1.0

Then watch the release workflow on the Actions tab. When it finishes, check the release page, and on a Mac:

brew update
brew install vinayhpandya/tap/rediska     # or: brew upgrade rediska
rediska --version

Tags follow semantic versioning: bump the last number for fixes (v0.1.1), the middle one for new features (v0.2.0). A tag with a suffix, like v0.2.0-rc1, is published as a pre-release.

docs.title: Trying it without publishing
docs.text:
Install GoReleaser, then:

goreleaser check                         # is .goreleaser.yaml valid?
goreleaser release --snapshot --clean    # build everything into dist/

A snapshot builds every archive and the cask file into dist/ (ignored by git), and publishes nothing. dist/homebrew/Casks/rediska.rb is the cask that would go to the tap.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
• The workflow fails at the Homebrew step: the GitHub Release is already published. Fix the token, then re-run the failed job from the Actions tab.
  • A bad release went out: delete the release and the tag on GitHub, then delete the tag locally (git tag -d v0.1.0), fix, and tag again. If the tap was already updated, the next release overwrites it.
  • macOS says the binary can't be opened: the binary isn't signed by Apple. The cask removes macOS's quarantine flag after installing, which needs a recent Homebrew (brew update). For a downloaded archive, run xattr -d com.apple.quarantine rediska once.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
go test ./...            # everything, including the 3-node end-to-end test
go test -short ./...     # fast unit tests only
go test -race ./...      # with Go's race detector, as CI runs them

To run one package or one test:

go test ./cluster/
go test ./commands/ -run TestCheckCluster -v

docs.title: What's tested where
docs.text: Package Tests cluster key slots (through the examples), parsing cluster.conf (including 9 kinds of broken file), slot ownership commands routing (MOVED, CROSSSLOT, CLUSTERDOWN, hash tags), CLUSTER replies, AOF replay, out-of-memory, PFADD errors server MULTI/EXEC in cluster mode, with the replies real Redis gives store PFADD key counts and memory accounting core RESP parsing e2e a real 3-node cluster, over TCP

docs.title: The end-to-end test
docs.text:
e2e/cluster_test.go checks the whole cluster the way a client sees it:

  1. builds rediska into a temporary folder,
  2. picks three free ports and writes a layout for them,
  3. starts three real rediska processes,
  4. sends commands over TCP and checks every reply: redirects, hash tags, pipelines, transactions and CLUSTER SLOTS,
  5. stops the nodes and deletes everything, even if a check fails.

It takes a couple of seconds, mostly for the build, and go test -short skips it.

docs.title: Examples are tests too
docs.text:
Functions named Example... in _test.go files appear in the API docs as usage examples, and go test runs them and checks their output against the // Output: comment. For example, from cluster/example_test.go:

func ExampleKeyHashSlot() {
    fmt.Println(cluster.KeyHashSlot("name"))
    fmt.Println(cluster.KeyHashSlot("{user1}.name"), cluster.KeyHashSlot("{user1}.email"))
    // Output:
    // 5798
    // 8106 8106
}

If the code changes so the output no longer matches, the test fails, so the examples in the docs can't go out of date.

docs.title: Comparing with real Redis
docs.text:
Many expected replies in the tests were first recorded from a real Redis 7 server, so Rediska's behaviour matches it word for word. To compare by hand, run a real Redis next to Rediska:

redis-server --port 6390 --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file /tmp/nodes-6390.conf
for k in name age visits "{user1}.name"; do
  echo "$k  redis=$(redis-cli -p 6390 cluster keyslot "$k")  rediska=$(redis-cli -p 7001 cluster keyslot "$k")"
done

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Every push to main and every pull request runs, on Linux and macOS:

  1. a gofmt check (fails if any file isn't formatted),
  2. go vet ./...,
  3. go build ./...,
  4. go test -race ./....

See .github/workflows/ci.yaml. A separate workflow builds and publishes this documentation site, and pushing a version tag runs the release workflow (see Releasing).

docs.title: func KeyHashSlot
docs.text:
func KeyHashSlot(key string) int

KeyHashSlot returns the slot (0..16383) a key belongs to.

Hash tags: if the key contains "{" followed later by "}" with at least one character between them, only the part inside the FIRST such pair is hashed. That lets clients force related keys into one slot, e.g. "{user1000}.following" and "{user1000}.followers". An empty tag "{}" means the whole key is hashed.

Example

Every key maps to one of 16384 slots. Keys that share a \{hash tag\} always land in the same slot, so they can be used together in one command. 

package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska/cluster"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Println(cluster.KeyHashSlot("name"))
    fmt.Println(cluster.KeyHashSlot("age"))
    fmt.Println(cluster.KeyHashSlot("{user1}.name"), cluster.KeyHashSlot("{user1}.email"))
}
#### Output 
5798
741
8106 8106

docs.text:
func (b *Bus) Meet(host string, port int) error

Meet is CLUSTER MEET: start a handshake with the node at host:port (its client port). We don't know its ID yet, so the peer gets a random one until the node's PONG tells us the real one (see renamePeer). tick connects to it, and the first message is a MEET, so it adds us too.

Meeting a node we already know, or ourselves, does nothing.

docs.title: func (*Bus) Start
docs.text:
func (b *Bus) Start(ctx context.Context, send func(Event))

Start starts the bus's goroutines; they run until ctx is cancelled. send must hand an event to dispatchWorker (which calls Handle), and must not block forever once ctx is cancelled.

Each goroutine waits for a different thing:

  • acceptLoop: another node connecting to us
  • cronLoop: the 100 ms timer
  • dialLoop: tick asking us to connect to a node
  • the last one: shutdown, to close the listener (which wakes acceptLoop)

A layout lists every node and the slots it owns. The node finds itself by its port, and Owner says which node serves a slot. 

package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska/cluster"

func main() {
    conf := `
node1  127.0.0.1:7001  0-5460
node2  127.0.0.1:7002  5461-10922
node3  127.0.0.1:7003  10923-16383

}

docs.title: func CheckCluster
docs.text:
func CheckCluster(cmd *Command) []byte

CheckCluster reports whether this node may run cmd in cluster mode. It returns nil if so (or if cluster mode is off), otherwise the error reply to send instead: CROSSSLOT, CLUSTERDOWN or MOVED.

The server package calls it while queuing commands inside MULTI. That happens on the connection's goroutine, not the dispatch worker, which is safe only because the cluster layout never changes after startup. Once slots can move at runtime, this must go through the worker or take a lock.

docs.title: func Dispatch
docs.text:
func Dispatch(cmd *Command) []byte

Dispatch runs one command and returns its encoded RESP reply.

It replies with an error, without running anything, if the command is unknown or, in cluster mode, if its keys span several slots (CROSSSLOT), belong to no node (CLUSTERDOWN) or belong to another node (MOVED).

For commands that can grow memory, and only when --maxmemory is set, it then evicts keys according to the policy, and replies with an OOM error without running the command if memory is still over the limit.

Otherwise it runs the handler, and appends successful write commands to the AOF if one is set (see SetAOF).

Dispatch must only be called from the dispatch worker goroutine.

docs.title: func DispatchBatch
docs.text:
func DispatchBatch(cmd []*Command) []byte

DispatchBatch runs the commands queued by MULTI when the client sends EXEC, and returns their replies wrapped in one RESP array.

In cluster mode, all keys of all the commands together must be in one slot owned by this node. If they aren't, DispatchBatch returns that single error (CROSSSLOT, CLUSTERDOWN or MOVED) and runs nothing, so a transaction never runs halfway.

docs.title: func DispatchPipeline
docs.text:
func DispatchPipeline(cmds []*Command) []byte

DispatchPipeline runs each command in order and returns their replies concatenated back-to-back -- exactly as if each had been dispatched and written individually, one at a time. Unlike DispatchBatch (used for MULTI/EXEC, which needs one array-wrapped reply representing the whole transaction), pipelined commands each need their own independent, individually-parseable reply, so no outer array framing is added here.

docs.title: func IsKnownCommand
docs.text:
func IsKnownCommand(name string) bool

IsKnownCommand reports whether a command called name (upper case) has been registered. MULTI uses it to reject unknown commands when they are queued, rather than at EXEC.

docs.title: func KeysOf
docs.text:
func KeysOf(cmd *Command) (keys []string, ok bool)

KeysOf returns the key arguments of cmd. ok is false if the command has no key spec (i.e. it is unknown). Too few arguments just yields fewer keys; the handler itself reports the arity error.

docs.title: func Register
docs.text:
func Register(name string, f HandlerFunc)

Register adds a command. name must be upper case, since Dispatch looks commands up by their upper-cased name. Registering a name twice replaces the earlier handler. Command files call Register from their init function.

docs.title: func Replay
docs.text:
func Replay(cmd *Command)

Replay runs a command read back from the AOF at startup. Unlike Dispatch, it skips the cluster check and the memory check, and doesn't write to the AOF: everything in this node's AOF was already accepted by this node, so it must all be loaded back, even if the cluster layout has changed since. Unknown commands are ignored.

docs.title: func SetAOF
docs.text:
func SetAOF(a *core.AOF)

SetAOF makes Dispatch append successful write commands to a. Call it only after the AOF has been replayed at startup; otherwise every replayed command would be written to the file a second time.

docs.text:
Command is one parsed client request, such as SET name vinay.

    Name string // uppercased for case-insensitive lookup
    Args []string

docs.text:
func ParseCommand(decoded any) (*Command, error)

ParseCommand turns a value decoded by core.Decode into a Command. The value must be a non-empty array of bulk strings; the first one becomes the upper-cased command name.

docs.title: type HandlerFunc
docs.text:
HandlerFunc runs one command. args are the command's arguments without the command name, and the return value is the full encoded RESP reply.

type HandlerFunc func(args []string) []byte

docs.title: type KeySpec
docs.text:
KeySpec says which arguments of a command are keys, using the same scheme as Redis's command table. Positions index the full argv, where argv[0] is the command name itself:

First: position of the first key (0 = the command takes no keys)
Last:  position of the last key; negative counts from the end, so -1
       means "the last argument"
Step:  distance between keys (1 = every argument in range is a key)

Examples: GET k -> {1,1,1}; DEL k1 k2 k3 -> {1,-1,1}; OBJECT ENCODING k -> {2,2,1}.

type KeySpec struct {
    First, Last, Step int
}

docs.title: func Decode
docs.text:
func Decode(r *bufio.Reader) (any, error)

Decode parses one RESP value from r. Each call that reaches a bulk string allocates its own buffer — fine for occasional/one-shot use (e.g. AOF replay, tests). For decoding many commands in a row from the same connection, use NewDecoder instead to reuse a scratch buffer across calls.

docs.title: func DecodeInteger
docs.text:
func DecodeInteger(b []byte) (int64, error)

DecodeInteger parses an encoded RESP integer reply, such as ":42\r\n", back into a number. The server uses it to read replies it produced itself, such as the active-expiry loop's count of deleted keys.

docs.title: func EncodeArray
docs.text:
func EncodeArray(args []string) []byte

EncodeArray encodes args as a RESP array of bulk strings, the format clients use to send commands: SET k v becomes "*3 $3 SET $1 k $1 v ". To build an array of other kinds of values, use EncodeRawArray.

Example

EncodeArray is the format clients use to send commands. 

package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska/core"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Printf("%q
", core.EncodeArray([]string{"SET", "name", "vinay"}))
}
#### Output 
"*3
$3
SET
$4
name
$5
vinay
"

docs.title: func EncodeBulkString
docs.text:
func EncodeBulkString(s string) []byte

EncodeBulkString encodes s as a RESP bulk string, such as "$5\r\nvinay\r\n". Bulk strings may contain any bytes, including newlines.

Example

The encoders return raw RESP bytes; %q shows the \\r\\n line endings. 

package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska/core"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", core.EncodeBulkString("vinay"))
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", core.EncodeSimpleString("OK"))
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", core.EncodeInteger(42))
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", core.EncodeNullBulkString())
}
#### Output 
"$5\r\nvinay\r\n"
"+OK\r\n"
":42\r\n"
"$-1\r\n"

docs.title: func EncodeError
docs.text:
func EncodeError(s string) []byte

EncodeError encodes s as a RESP error reply, such as "-ERR unknown command\r\n". By convention s starts with an error code in capitals (ERR, MOVED, CROSSSLOT, ...), which clients use to tell errors apart.

docs.title: func EncodeInteger
docs.text:
func EncodeInteger(n int64) []byte

EncodeInteger encodes n as a RESP integer, such as ":42\r\n".

docs.title: func EncodeNullBulkString
docs.text:
func EncodeNullBulkString() []byte

EncodeNullBulkString returns RESP's nil reply, "$-1\r\n", which means "no value", for example GET on a key that doesn't exist.

docs.title: func EncodeRawArray
docs.text:
func EncodeRawArray(items [][]byte) []byte

EncodeRawArray wraps items, each already RESP-encoded, in a RESP array. Because an encoded array is itself an item, calls can be nested to build arrays of arrays, as CLUSTER SLOTS does. A nil or empty items gives the empty array "*0\r\n".

Example

EncodeRawArray takes already\-encoded items, so it can mix types and nest arrays. This builds \[0, 5460, \["127.0.0.1", 7001\]\]. 

package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska/core"
)

func main() {
    owner := core.EncodeRawArray([][]byte{
        core.EncodeBulkString("127.0.0.1"),
        core.EncodeInteger(7001),
    })
    reply := core.EncodeRawArray([][]byte{
        core.EncodeInteger(0),
        core.EncodeInteger(5460),
        owner,
    })
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", reply)
}
#### Output 
"*3\r\n:0\r\n:5460\r\n*2\r\n$9\r\n127.0.0.1\r\n:7001\r\n"

func EncodeSimpleString(s string) []byte

EncodeSimpleString encodes s as a RESP simple string, such as "+OK\r\n". s must not contain \r or \n; use EncodeBulkString for arbitrary text.

func (a *AOF) Close() error

docs.title: func (*AOF) Recover
docs.text:
func (a *AOF) Recover(fn func(args []string)) error

Recover replays the file from the beginning, calling fn with each command's arguments, name first. Entries that aren't arrays are skipped. It stops quietly at the first entry it can't decode, so a file cut short by a crash still loads every complete command before that point. It only returns an error if it can't move to the start of the file.

docs.text:
func (a *AOF) Sync() error

Sync flushes the file to disk with fsync. Until then, recent writes may only be in the operating system's cache and can be lost if the machine crashes. The server calls Sync when it shuts down.

Write appends one command, such as ["SET", "name", "vinay"], to the file as a RESP array. It doesn't call Sync.

docs.text:
import "github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska/server"

Package server runs Rediska's network side: it accepts TCP connections, reads commands, and sends replies.

Each client connection has its own goroutine, which parses commands and handles MULTI/EXEC queuing and pipelining. Every command that touches data is sent over a channel to one dispatch worker goroutine, which runs commands one at a time. That's how Rediska keeps Redis's single-threaded guarantee: commands never run at the same time, so the store needs no locks.

docs.title: func Run
docs.text:
func Run(ctx context.Context, host string, port int, appendOnly bool, appendFilename string) error

Run starts the server and blocks until ctx is cancelled.

If appendOnly is true, it first opens appendFilename and replays it to restore the data. It then listens on host:port, starts the dispatch worker and the active-expiry loop, and serves each connection on its own goroutine.

When ctx is cancelled it shuts down cleanly: it stops accepting connections, waits for the open ones to finish, lets the worker run every command already queued, then syncs and closes the AOF. It returns an error only if startup fails (opening or replaying the AOF, or listening).

import "github.com/vinayhpandya/rediska/store"

Package store holds Rediska's data: an in-memory map from keys to values, with expiry, memory accounting and eviction (LRU or LFU).

Values are kept in compact encodings, as in Redis: integers as numbers, strings as SDS, HyperLogLogs as sketches (see Encoding).

A Store is not safe for concurrent use. The server only touches Default from its single dispatch worker goroutine.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
LRU clock constants. The clock is a 24-bit value that ticks once per second and wraps back to zero roughly every 194 days, mirroring Redis.

const (
    LRUClockMax        = (1 << 24) - 1 // 16777215
    LRUClockResolution = 1000          // milliseconds per tick (1 second)
    EvictionPoolSize   = 16            // candidates kept across eviction cycles

)

LFU reuses the same 24-bit `entry.lru` field that LRU uses, exactly like real Redis reuses its `robj.lru:24` bitfield. The two policies are never active on the same key at the same time (maxmemory-policy is global), so no extra struct field is needed:

bits 8-23 (16 bits): ldt  -- last-decay time, in minutes, wraps ~45 days
bits 0-7  (8 bits):  counter -- logarithmic access counter, 0-255

const (
    LFUInitVal uint8 = 5 // starting counter for a freshly written key

)

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
LFULogFactor and LFUDecayTime are runtime-tunable (unlike LFUInitVal, which real Redis also keeps fixed). They default to Redis's own defaults and are overridden via SetLFUParams, called from main.go once config flags are parsed.

var (
    LFULogFactor uint32 = 10 // higher = slower counter growth (config: lfu-log-factor)
    LFUDecayTime uint32 = 1  // minutes per decay step (config: lfu-decay-time)
)

Default is the global store instance. Never access this directly — always go through the command worker.

var Default = New()

ErrNotHLL is returned when a HyperLogLog command is used on a key that holds some other kind of value. The text matches Redis's reply.

var ErrNotHLL = errors.New("WRONGTYPE Key is not a valid HyperLogLog string value.")

ErrWrongType is returned when a command is used on a key that holds the wrong kind of value. The text matches Redis's reply.

var ErrWrongType = errors.New("WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value")

KeyspaceStat holds the counters INFO keyspace reports, one map per database (only database 0 is used). Only "keys" is kept up to date so far; "expires" and "avg_ttl" are read by INFO but always 0.

var KeyspaceStat [4]map[string]int

func (s *Store) Append(key, value string) (int64, error)

Append implements Redis's APPEND: creates the key if it doesn't exist (identical to a SET with no TTL), otherwise appends to the existing value. An INT-encoded key is converted to its string form first and becomes RAW-encoded afterward — same as real Redis. Returns the new total length, matching Redis's APPEND reply.

An expired key counts as missing. A key holding a HyperLogLog is left unchanged and ErrWrongType is returned.

docs.title: func (*Store) DeleteExpired
docs.text:
func (s *Store) DeleteExpired() int

DeleteExpired does one round of active expiry: it checks up to 20 keys that have an expiry, picked in Go's random map order, removes those that have expired, and returns how many it removed. The server runs it every 100 ms and repeats while a round still finds 5 or more expired keys.

docs.text:
func (s *Store) Get(key string) (string, bool)

Get returns key's value as a string, and whether the key exists. An expired key is removed and reported as missing. It counts as an access for LRU/LFU. A key holding a HyperLogLog is also reported as missing, whereas real Redis would return its raw bytes.

docs.title: func (*Store) GetEncoding
docs.text:
func (s *Store) GetEncoding(key string) (Encoding, bool)

docs.title: func (*Store) GetFreq
docs.text:
func (s *Store) GetFreq(key string) (freq uint8, ok bool, policyOK bool)

GetFreq returns a key's LFU counter (used by OBJECT FREQ), same as real Redis. It's a metadata read and does NOT bump recency. ok is false if the key doesn't exist, and policyOK is false if the active policy isn't an LFU policy -- callers should surface that as a distinct error, mirroring Redis's "An LFU maxmemory policy is not selected" response.

docs.text:
func (s *Store) GetInt(key string) (int64, bool, error, time.Time)

GetInt returns key's value as an integer, for commands like INCR. The results are the value, whether the key exists, an error if it exists but doesn't hold an integer, and the key's expiry time (zero if none). It counts as an access for LRU/LFU.

docs.title: func (*Store) PFAdd
docs.text:
func (s *Store) PFAdd(key string, values ...string) (changed bool, err error)

PFAdd adds values to the HyperLogLog at key, creating it if needed. It reports whether anything changed: creating the key counts as a change, even with no values, as in Redis. If key holds some other kind of value, PFAdd changes nothing and returns ErrNotHLL.

docs.title: func (*Store) PFCount
docs.text:
func (s *Store) PFCount(keys ...string) (int64, error)

PFCount returns the estimated number of distinct values in the HyperLogLogs at keys. With one key, that's its own count; with several, it's the count of their union, computed in a temporary sketch without storing anything, as in Redis. Missing or expired keys count as empty. If any key holds some other kind of value, it returns ErrNotHLL.

docs.title: func (*Store) PFMerge
docs.text:
func (s *Store) PFMerge(dest string, sources ...string) error

PFMerge stores in dest the union of the HyperLogLogs at dest and every source key. Missing or expired keys count as empty. If dest already exists it keeps its expiry, as in Redis.

Every key is checked before anything changes: if any of them holds some other kind of value, PFMerge returns ErrNotHLL and changes nothing.

PerformEvictions frees keys until the store is back under maxBytes. It runs only inside the single command worker, so it needs no locks.

docs.text:
func (s *Store) Set(key, value string, ttl time.Duration)

Set stores value under key, replacing any old value and its expiry. If ttl is greater than zero the key expires after ttl; otherwise it never expires. The value is stored as an integer if it parses as one, and as a string otherwise.

func (s *Store) SetPolicy(policy string)

SetPolicy sets the maxmemory policy, which decides how keys are evicted and whether keys track recency (LRU) or frequency (LFU). It is called once at startup.

docs.title: func New

func New() *HLL

New creates an empty HLL, starting in sparse form: a single XZERO opcode covering all 16384 registers, exactly like a fresh Redis HLL.

docs.title: func (*HLL) Add
docs.text:
func (h *HLL) Add(data []byte) bool

Add hashes data and updates the relevant register if this element produced a longer run of leading zeros than previously seen there. Returns true if the register (and therefore the estimate) changed.

docs.title: func (*HLL) Count
docs.text:
func (h *HLL) Count() uint64

Count returns the estimated cardinality, using the harmonic-mean estimator with the standard low-cardinality linear-counting correction. (Large-range bias correction is omitted here since a 64-bit hash never approaches the collision range that requires it.)

If no register has changed since the last call, the cached result is returned directly without rescanning -- this is the common case, since most Add calls don't actually beat an existing register's max value.

docs.title: func (*HLL) Encoding
docs.text:
func (h *HLL) Encoding() string

Encoding reports which representation is currently active ("sparse" or "dense") -- mirrors Redis's PFDEBUG ENCODING, mainly useful for tests and debugging.

docs.title: func (*HLL) Merge
docs.text:
func (h *HLL) Merge(other *HLL) bool

Merge folds other's registers into h via an elementwise max -- this is the same operation Redis's PFMERGE (and multi-key PFCOUNT, on a scratch copy) performs. The result always ends up dense (h is promoted first if it was sparse), matching how Redis computes merges internally rather than trying to splice two sparse streams together. Returns true if any register in h changed.
